title: Custom validation for domain invariants / Expected API failures with HTTPException

blocks.text: Individually valid fields can still form an invalid booking. Use @model_validator(mode="after") on an instance method to inspect multiple already-validated fields. Raise ValueError when the invariant fails; return self on success.
For a custom check on one already-validated field, use @field_validator('field', mode='after') with a @classmethod, returning the validated field value when accepted.
Test the relationship with individually valid values that violate it: model construction must raise ValidationError. Also test that a consistent pair is accepted.

annotations.text: After-model instance method inspects already-validated fields.
Successful validator returns the model instance.
Individually typed pairs isolate the relationship; compare inconsistent and consistent inputs. Evaluate construction separately for each case.

blocks.text: The exercise requires end to be later than start. An after-model validator checks their already-validated values, raises ValueError for an inconsistent pair and returns self for a consistent pair. Construction reports the invariant failure as ValidationError.

A single-field after-validator instead uses a classmethod and returns the accepted field value. Do not demonstrate a cross-field rule with an input that already fails its field type; that tests a different boundary.

segments.label: Check a password-confirmation invariant after field validation
segments.summary: A registration model contains email, password and confirmation fields. A model validator compares the two password fields after individual field validation. It receives self, giving it access to the model instance rather than just one value, and does not use the classmethod decorator used for field validators. Constructing the model with two different password strings produces a validation error reporting that the passwords do not match.

bridge.before: Watch how the validator receives the whole instance after individual field validation. The clip checks password confirmation using a mismatched pair; our booking example applies the same cross-field principle.
bridge.after: The clip demonstrates a mismatch failure. The text also covers returning self on success, the complete single-field validator pattern, and verifying both rejection of individually valid but inconsistent inputs and acceptance of consistent inputs.

public.prompt: Booking requires end > start after both integer fields have validated. Where should this relationship be checked?

options.text: An after-model instance validator comparing self.end and self.start.
No custom check: successful integer conversion proves end > start.
A field validator that checks only whether end is an integer.

blocks.text: An absent order is an expected rejection, not a successful result containing an exception object. Raise HTTPException(status_code=..., detail=...) to stop normal operation work and produce the intended HTTP rejection.
FastAPI’s default rejection body places the supplied value under the JSON key detail. Supply headers on the exception when response metadata is required, such as an authentication challenge.
Review the status, detail structure and required headers. Raising marks the control-flow boundary; returning the exception object does not express the same instruction.

annotations.text: Absent-order rejection: status 404; normal work stops here. FastAPI places the supplied value under the default JSON key detail.
Only the non-rejected path reaches this return.

blocks.text: When the order is absent under the contract, raise HTTPException with the intended status and client-facing detail. The raise stops normal work and produces the rejection; returning the object is not equivalent.
The default body uses the key detail. If the rejection needs metadata, pass headers to the exception. Keep the detail client-facing rather than exposing internal diagnostics.

steps.title: Check: Expected API failures with HTTPException

public.prompt: An absent order requires a deliberate HTTP rejection. Which action stops the operation with that rejection?

options.text: Return the HTTPException object as a normal result.
Raise HTTPException with the intended status_code and detail.
Create an HTTPException object but continue returning the normal result.

o1.message: Returning the exception object is not the taught rejection control flow: raise it.

o2.message: Raise HTTPException(status_code=..., detail=...) to stop the operation and return a deliberate HTTP rejection rather than returning the exception object.

o3.message: Merely constructing an exception does not stop the operation; raising does.

correct.message: Raise HTTPException(status_code=..., detail=...) to stop the operation and return a deliberate HTTP rejection rather than returning the exception object.

incorrect.message: Review the distinction and try again. Raise HTTPException(status_code=..., detail=...) to stop the operation and return a deliberate HTTP rejection rather than returning the exception object.

hints: Distinguish constructing, returning and raising an exception.

steps.title: Check: Expected API failures with HTTPException

public.prompt: A deliberate rejection contract requires response metadata in a header. How should HTTPException carry that metadata?

options.text: Use its headers keyword with the required header name and value.
Return an HTTPException instead of raising it to turn detail into headers.
Put the header name only in the detail message.

o1.message: HTTPException accepts headers for required response metadata, such as an authentication challenge.

o2.message: The exception must be raised, and headers must be supplied explicitly rather than inferred from detail.

o3.message: detail is response detail, not the headers argument for required metadata.

correct.message: HTTPException accepts headers for required response metadata, such as an authentication challenge.

incorrect.message: Review the distinction and try again. HTTPException accepts headers for required response metadata, such as an authentication challenge.

hints: Separate body detail from response metadata.
